description: In a capitalist economy, the periodic and cyclical fluctuations in economic activities (like production, employment, and income) over time are called Business Cycles. Economic Growth, on the other hand, refers to the steady, long-term increase in a country's real productive capacity and output.

sections.title: Economic Growth vs. Economic Development
sections.description: While often used interchangeably, there is a fundamental distinction between economic growth and economic development in macroeconomics.

key_concepts.explanation: A quantitative concept that refers to the sustained increase in a country's real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) or per capita income over a specific period.

A broader qualitative concept that includes economic growth along with progressive changes in the socio-economic structure, such as improvements in health, education, life expectancy, and standard of living.

important_facts.fact: The Human Development Index (HDI), published annually by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), is the most widely used metric to measure economic development.
Economic growth can occur without economic development (often termed as 'Jobless Growth'), but economic development is impossible without economic growth.

sections.title: Major Phases of a Business Cycle
sections.description: A standard business cycle consists of recurring phases of upward and downward movements in macroeconomic variables, completing a full cycle.

key_concepts.explanation: A phase characterized by increasing employment, economic output, aggregate demand, and easy availability of bank credit. Business profits and investments rise.
The highest point of the business cycle where the economy is producing at maximum capacity. This phase is often accompanied by high inflation and resource bottlenecks.

A slowdown in economic activity characterized by falling demand and rising unemployment. If an economy experiences negative GDP growth for two consecutive quarters, it is termed a 'Technical Recession'.
The lowest point of the cycle where economic activity bottoms out. A severe, widespread, and prolonged recession turns into a depression.
The phase where the economy bounces back from the trough, usually aided by government stimulus or central bank interventions (like cutting interest rates) to boost investment and consumption.

sections.title: Macroeconomic Indicators
sections.description: Economists and policymakers rely on specific statistical indicators to track, measure, and predict the stages of a business cycle.

key_concepts.explanation: Variables that change before the overall economy changes, helping to predict future economic trends. Examples include Stock Market indices, Bond Yields, and new manufacturing orders.
Variables that change after the economy has already begun to follow a particular pattern. They confirm a long-term trend. Examples include Unemployment Rate and Corporate Profits.
Variables that change simultaneously with the overall economic cycle, providing real-time data on the current state of the economy. Examples include Industrial Production and Personal Income.

key_associations.extra_info: An inverted U-shaped curve suggesting that as an economy develops, market forces first increase and then eventually decrease economic inequality.
An economic concept showing an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment in the short run.

sections.title: Theories of Economic Growth and Historical Events
sections.description: Various economic models have been developed to explain the drivers of long-term economic growth, often shaped by historical global crises.

key_concepts.explanation: A model suggesting that economic growth depends primarily on the national savings rate and the capital-output ratio. India's First Five-Year Plan was heavily based on this framework.
A neo-classical model stating that long-run economic growth is driven by capital accumulation, labor force expansion, and most importantly, technological progress.

historical_events.significance: The most severe economic depression in modern history. It led to the rise of 'Keynesian Economics' by John Maynard Keynes, which advocated for increased government expenditure to stimulate demand during downturns.
Triggered by the subprime mortgage crisis in the USA, leading to a severe global recession, a credit freeze, and massive government bailouts of the banking system.

sections.title: Shapes of Economic Recovery
sections.description: The trajectory and speed at which an economy recovers from a recession is often described graphically using letter shapes.

key_concepts.explanation: A sharp economic decline followed immediately by a quick and strong recovery. This is considered the best-case scenario for an economy.
A sharp decline followed by a period of stagnation at the bottom (trough) for several quarters or years before gradually recovering.
Also known as a 'Double-dip Recession'. The economy begins to recover from a recession but falls back into another downturn before fully recovering.

A scenario where different sectors, industries, or income groups recover at vastly different rates (e.g., technology sectors boom while hospitality continues to decline), exacerbating economic inequality.
